lesson.title: Ranking the Invisible Forces
lesson.summary: Comparing London dispersion, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding, and ion-dipole forces on a single scale reveals a general strength ranking, along with an important exception when large or highly polarizable molecules are involved.
lesson.body:
With London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces, hydrogen bonding, and ion-dipole forces all covered individually, the natural next step is to line them up and compare their relative strengths. For molecules of roughly similar size, the general ranking from weakest to strongest is dispersion forces, then dipole-dipole forces, then hydrogen bonding, then ion-dipole forces. This order tracks how concentrated and permanent the charge separation is: dispersion forces rely on brief, randomly fluctuating charge imbalances; dipole-dipole forces involve a small, permanent but partial charge separation; hydrogen bonding is a special, unusually strong case of dipole-dipole attraction restricted to H bonded to N, O, or F; and ion-dipole forces involve one side carrying a full, permanent unit charge, which no partial-charge interaction can match.

A clean way to see this ranking is by comparing boiling points of small molecules while noting molar mass, since a heavier molecule tends to have stronger dispersion forces on its own. Methane (CH4, molar mass 16, dispersion only) boils at minus 162 degrees Celsius. Formaldehyde (H2CO, molar mass 30, dipole-dipole) boils at minus 19 degrees Celsius, well above methane even though it is the heavier molecule, showing dipole-dipole attraction adding real pull beyond dispersion alone. Water (H2O, molar mass 18, hydrogen bonding) boils at 100 degrees Celsius, dramatically higher again despite being lighter than formaldehyde and barely heavier than methane, a strong sign that hydrogen bonding is doing far more work than molar mass could explain. Dissolved ionic compounds have no boiling point of their own to compare directly, but the energy needed to separate Na+ from Cl- and fully hydrate each ion, the process ion-dipole forces drive, is substantially larger than the energy needed to separate hydrogen-bonded water molecules, consistent with ion-dipole forces sitting at the top of the scale.

This ranking comes with an important and frequently tested caveat: it assumes molecules of comparable size. London dispersion forces grow rapidly with the number of electrons and the polarizability of a molecule, meaning how easily its electron cloud can be distorted into a temporary dipole. A large, easily polarizable nonpolar molecule can have dispersion forces that outweigh the dipole-dipole forces or even the hydrogen bonding of a much smaller polar molecule. Iodine, I2, is nonpolar and interacts only through dispersion forces, yet it is a solid at room temperature with a melting point of 114 degrees Celsius, because its many electrons make it highly polarizable. By contrast, hydrogen fluoride, HF, hydrogen bonds, yet it boils at only about 19.5 degrees Celsius. The takeaway is not that dispersion forces are secretly the strongest type of force in general, but that molecular size and polarizability can outweigh the type of force present when comparing two very differently sized molecules.

The practical strategy for comparing two substances is therefore two-step: identify which force types each substance is capable of (checking specifically for the hydrogen bond requirement of H bonded to N, O, or F, and for the presence of ions), then weigh those force types against molecular size and polarizability rather than assuming the general ranking automatically wins. When comparable in size, hydrogen bonding beats plain dipole-dipole, which beats dispersion alone, and ion-dipole beats all three; when sizes differ substantially, dispersion forces can climb high enough to compete with or exceed the others.
